# Machine learning

Models small enough to train inside a box, in plain Kotlin, while you watch. Flow matching carries one 2D or 3D point cloud onto another and hands back the deformation between them; the multi-output regression head it trains is usable on its own. See [Flow Matching](../flow_matching.md).

A whole task handed to Field's own agent: a goal, a document, a tool-round budget, and checks that decide — from the document and what its boxes said, not from the agent's final text — whether the goal was met.

## AgentTaskTranscript.kt { #agenttasktranscript-kt }

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/agent/AgentTaskTranscript.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/agent/AgentTaskTranscript/)

### AgentTaskTranscript { #agenttasktranscript-kt-agenttasktranscript }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">object</span> <span class="nc">AgentTaskTranscript</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/agent/AgentTaskTranscript/#L23)

Writes an agent task into a box's AI4 chat transcript (`ai4_chat_history`), in the transcript's own markup (`<<you>>`, `<<ai>>`, `<<progress>>`, `<<model:…>>`), and pushes it to the box's `ai-chat` panel. The panel then renders the task like any other turn, and the person can continue the conversation from there.

### FieldGraphHost { #fieldgraphtools-kt-fieldgraphhost }

### InFieldAgentEvals { #infieldagentevals-kt-infieldagentevals }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">object</span> <span class="nc">InFieldAgentEvals</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/agent/InFieldAgentEvals/#L19)

A small eval suite for Field's own agent: seventeen tasks (five graded by pixels, three made of many similar calls that a tool program does in one, two that are several turns of one conversation), each a goal, the setup it starts from, checks that decide it, and a scripted solution.

Chart's container has class `bars`, and *another* box, Theme, displays a stylesheet that makes `.bars` `flex-direction: row-reverse` — output panels share one page, so a style in one panel reaches every other. The bars therefore appear in the reverse of the list's order, and sorting the list ascending, the obvious first move, draws them tallest-first. Chart's own code does not say so; the picture does. (The first version put row-reverse in Chart's own code; the live model read it and got it right first time, twice, so it tested nothing.) The scripted solution makes the mistake on purpose, sees it, and fixes it. |

### FieldBuildInfo { #aisessiontree-kt-fieldbuildinfo }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">object</span> <span class="nc">FieldBuildInfo</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/conversation/AiSessionTree/#L555)

Which Field this is: the checkout's commit, whether the tree was dirty, and a hash of the diff — what a capability checkpoint records so a transcript says which code its tools ran on. Read once, in the background, from `git` in the working directory (a packaged build may ship `field-build-info.properties` instead, which wins). Not a Gradle-generated resource: one that changes on every commit would make every test task out of date.

### Kept { #contextpipeline-kt-kept }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">enum</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">Kept</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">label</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/conversation/ContextPipeline/#L146)

Where a fragment ends up, given where the bridge put it (`ContextReport.placement`). The fragment classes describe intent; the provider decides retention, and these differ: OpenAI's conversations live on its side, so anything sent inside one stays there.

## TurnSuspension.kt { #turnsuspension-kt }

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ai/conversation/TurnSuspension.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/conversation/TurnSuspension/)

### SuspendsTurn { #turnsuspension-kt-suspendsturn }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">interface</span> <span class="nc">SuspendsTurn</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/conversation/TurnSuspension/#L14)

A tool result that ends the model's turn when `suspension` is set: the bridge finishes the round it is in, makes no further model request, and returns the suspension in [`OpenAiIdeCodexBridge.SendResult`](internal.md#actors-kt-sendresult). Someone else resumes the conversation later (`StudyBuildAwaits` for `AwaitStudyBuildsRequest`), so the time spent waiting costs no model calls.

### SuspendedRound { #turnsuspension-kt-suspendedround }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">SuspendedRound</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">outputs</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">PendingToolOutput</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/conversation/TurnSuspension/#L51)

The tool outputs of the round that suspended a turn, which the provider has not seen yet. The next turn sends them first: on OpenAI's chained responses its `previous_response_id` is still the response that made these calls, and every call must have an output before anything else can follow it; on Anthropic, whose history this bridge keeps, the `tool_use` blocks need their `tool_result`s in the next user message.

### ConsoleMute { #logging-kt-consolemute }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">object</span> <span class="nc">ConsoleMute</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/diagnostics/Logging/#L119)

Channels suppressed from the console — both the plain [`StdoutLog`](machine-learning.md#logging-kt-stdoutlog) and the interactive PinnedConsole honor this. Muted events still reach every *other* sink (e.g. the LogStream web widget), so nothing is lost; they're just too chatty for the terminal. Default mutes the chatty background channels (`info,boxes`, `info,persist`, `info,ai.boxnames`, `debug,boxes`). Override with `-Dafield.log.mute=...` or `AFIELD_LOG_MUTE=...` (semicolon-separated exact channel strings); set to a blank/empty value to mute nothing.

## deepsets.kt { #deepsets-kt }

A learned two-body interaction: the acceleration on a particle as a function of the neighbours
around it, fitted by autodiff from examples of any rule that can already be evaluated.

`flowMatch` learns `v(x, t)`: where a particle should go given only where it is. That can carry
a cloud onto a shape, and it is blind to the other particles. An interaction is the other kind
of rule:

    a_i = phi( v_i, SUM_j psi(x_j - x_i, v_j - v_i), MEAN_j psi(...) )

two small networks and a reduction over neighbours. This is the Deep Sets form, and its
aggregation is permutation-invariant over any number of neighbours, so one set of weights works
for a particle with three neighbours and a particle with three hundred. Classical boids is *one
particular choice* of `psi` and `phi`, so the family contains it.

### Why both a sum and a mean

Reynolds separation is a **sum**: being crowded by twenty neighbours pushes harder than being
crowded by two. Alignment and cohesion are **means**, since they are averages of neighbour
velocity and position. A mean-only aggregator cannot represent separation at any width, and a
sum-only one makes alignment scale with crowding, so `phi` is fed both, at a cost of
`messageWidth` extra inputs. `DeepSetsWeights.sumScale` keeps the summed branch in a sane range.

### The feature map is where the physics goes

`psi` is not fed the raw offset. It is fed `interactionFeatures`: the offset and velocity
difference, plus the **unit direction scaled by a small radial basis**, `u*p` and `u*p^2`, where
`p` is a bounded proximity that rises as neighbours get close.

Separation goes as `1/r` over a four-hundred-fold range of `r`, and a `tanh` network cannot
form the *product* of a direction and a steep radial profile out of Cartesian components at any
practical width. Alignment and cohesion are plain means, and linear in the inputs, so they
survive the raw encoding. Measured by ablation against the flocking rule: fed raw Cartesian
offsets the model reproduces those two to a relative error of **0.036** and separation only to
**0.78**, which is barely better than predicting the average.

A radial interaction is a direction times a profile, so handing the network `u` already
multiplied by a couple of profile terms states the *form* of a two-body law rather than
transcribing boids. The profile's coefficients, the velocity dependence, and how the summed and
meaned branches combine are all still learned.

### Trained by [`afield.math.autodiff.ADTape`](math.md#autodiff-kt-adtape), not by Smile

Smile's MLP cannot express this: the gradient has to flow back through a sum over a
*variable-length* neighbour set, and `psi` is applied once per neighbour with shared weights.
`autodiff.kt` is reverse-mode over a tape, which handles it without knowing anything about
networks, since the tape records whatever the forward pass did. Cost is one forward and one
backward sweep per batch whatever the neighbour counts are.

### The weights come out as [`MlpWeights`](machine-learning.md#neuralparticles-kt-mlpweights)

Both halves are packaged in the same flat layout the flow-matching work already uses, so
`MlpWeights.glsl` emits them for the GPU unchanged and the parity machinery in
`four.neural-field-parity.smoke` applies to them without modification.

### DeepSetsWeights { #deepsets-kt-deepsetsweights }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">DeepSetsWeights</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">psi</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">MlpWeights</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">phi</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">MlpWeights</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">messageWidth</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">radius</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">velocityScale</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">accelScale</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">sumScale</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">minSeparation</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/learning/deepsets/#L137)

A trained interaction in the plain Cartesian form: `psi` and `phi`, the width of the message between them, and the five scales that normalise a neighbourhood into the networks and the answer back out to world units. [`EquivariantWeights`](machine-learning.md#deepsets-kt-equivariantweights) is the same model constrained so that rotating a neighbourhood rotates the answer with it.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |

## flowmatching.kt { #flowmatching-kt }

Flow matching over 2D and 3D point clouds — `flowMatch` trains a velocity field that carries one
distribution onto another, and the field it returns can be sampled, integrated part-way, or drawn.

The idea is small enough to state completely. Pick a point `x0` from where you are starting and a
point `x1` from where you want to end up, and declare that the straight line between them is the
path a particle should take: at time `t` it is at `xt = (1-t)·x0 + t·x1`, travelling at `x1 - x0`.
Now fit a network `v(x, t)` to that velocity by least squares over many random `(x0, x1, t)`
triples. No two straight lines agree where they cross, so the fit cannot reproduce any single one
of them; what it converges to is the *average* velocity through each point at each time, and
integrating that average from `t = 0` to `t = 1` transports the whole starting distribution onto
the whole target one. That is the entire trick, and it is why there is no adversary, no sampler in
the training loop, and nothing to diverge — the loss is a plain regression MSE.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val target = flowSamples(myLine, 600, jitter = 4.0)   // sampled FLine + noise
val field = flowMatch(target, options = FlowMatchOptions(steps = 6000))
val cloud = field.sample(600)                         // fresh points from the same shape
val threads = field.paths(80)                         // the trajectories, as FLines
```

With a `from` cloud supplied it becomes a morph instead of a generator, and
`FlowMatchField.transport` runs the ODE only part-way: `transport(a, to = 0.5)` is a genuine
half-way shape rather than a vertex-wise average of two point lists.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val morph = flowMatch(to = flowSamples(lineB, 600), from = flowSamples(lineA, 600))
val halfway = morph.transport(flowSamples(lineA, 600), to = 0.5)
```

### Coordinates

Training happens in a normalised frame — the target cloud (both clouds, for a morph) is centred
and isotropically scaled to roughly unit variance — because a Gaussian source has to be
commensurate with the data for any of this to work, and FLine coordinates are usually in the
hundreds. The scaling is a single factor rather than per-axis, so it cannot squash a shape's aspect
ratio. [`FlowMatchField`](machine-learning.md#flowmatching-kt-flowmatchfield) converts at its boundary, so everything you pass in and get back is in the
coordinates you started with.

2D and 3D are distinguished by the data, not by a flag: a cloud whose `z` never varies is trained
as a 2D problem and its points come back on that same `z` plane. Pass `FlowMatchOptions.dimension`
to override. It matters — a 2D shape trained as 3D gets a Gaussian's worth of spread in `z` that
the field then has to learn to collapse.

### What this is not

- **Not a big model.** The default is two hidden layers of 64 `leaky` units trained by RMSProp,
  which is right for a few thousand points in two or three dimensions and nothing like enough for
  images. Training is single-threaded and per-sample (Smile's MLP has no batched matmul), so cost
  scales with `steps × batch`; see the timings in `FlowMatchingTest`.
- **Not able to change topology.** Integrating a velocity field is a continuous invertible map, so
  it cannot tear a loop open or join two strands into one — a flow can only deform. With
  `FlowCoupling.PAIRED` this stops being an abstraction and starts being the dominant error term:
  asking a straight segment to become a closed ring makes the mean landing error fifteen times
  worse than asking a small circle to do it, because the two ends of the segment are pulled to the
  same place and their paths have to cross. Give a closed target a closed source.
- **Not exact.** The field is an average over crossing paths, so samples land *near* the target
  distribution, not on it. Sharp corners smooth off, and thin structure needs more `steps` and more
  `hidden` before it resolves. `FlowMatchField.loss` is the training MSE, which measures the velocity
  fit and not the quality of the samples — judge those by looking, or with `chamferDistance`.
- **Not ordered.** `FlowMatchField.sample` returns an unordered cloud. Recovering an FLine from it is a
  separate problem; `FlowMatchField.transport` sidesteps it by moving points you already have, which
  keeps whatever order they came in.
- **Not conditional.** There is no class label or text prompt input — one field carries one
  distribution onto one other.

The knobs `flowMatch` takes, bundled so that a call that only wants to change one of them does not have to name the rest positionally.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">steps</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | Gradient steps to take. The dominant cost and the dominant quality lever. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">batch</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | Samples per gradient step. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">hidden</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">IntArray</span></code> | Hidden layer widths. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">activation</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code> | Hidden activation: `leaky`, `relu`, `tanh`, `sigmoid` or `linear`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">learningRate</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | RMSProp learning rate at the first step. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">finalLearningRate</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | Learning rate at the last step, decayed linearly from `learningRate`; null to hold it constant. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">momentum</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Momentum, or 0 to disable. **`flowMatch` refuses it unless `rho` is 0.** |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">rho</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | RMSProp decay, or 0 to fall back to plain SGD. See `momentum` before changing either. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">timeFeatures</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | How many `sin`/`cos` octaves of the time input the network sees, on top of raw `t`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">coupling</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">FlowCoupling</span></code> | How `x0` is paired with `x1`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">jitter</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Standard deviation of noise added to each drawn data point, in input coordinates. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">seed</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Long</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | Seed for the training draws. `null` takes an unpredictable one. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">dimension</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | Override the inferred 2-or-3 dimensionality. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">onProgress</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="p">(</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="nc">Unit</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | Called every `progressEvery` steps with the step index and the running mean loss. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">progressEvery</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | How often `onProgress` fires. |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">override</span> <span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">equals</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">other</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Any</span><span class="o">?</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/learning/flowmatching/#L516) | Two option sets are equal when they print the same. `hidden` is an `IntArray`, which compares by identity, so the equality a data class generates would call two identical settings different. |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">override</span> <span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">hashCode</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/learning/flowmatching/#L520) | Hashes the same string `equals` compares, so equal option sets land in the same bucket. |

Box-scoped Kotlin code tools (CompileKotlin, EvaluateKotlin), extracted from the ai-assist chat handler so the OpenAI harness and the MCP backdoor share one implementation. Context is supplied via four closures; everything else resolves to the promoted top-level helpers above. `refResolver` replaces the chat handler's `exec`-coupled `requestedRefOrCurrent` — the backdoor passes an explicit-target resolver with no "current box" fallback.

## AnthropicCredentials.kt { #anthropiccredentials-kt }

Credential + client construction for the Anthropic (Claude) provider.

Field's enterprise setup can't mint a raw `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, so the default
path here authenticates the way the official clients do: a short-lived OAuth
bearer token minted from an `ant auth login` profile via
`ant auth print-credentials --access-token`, sent as `Authorization: Bearer`
plus the `anthropic-beta: oauth-2025-04-20` header. A real API key
(`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`) or a pre-supplied bearer token (`ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`)
are honored first when present, so nothing here is `ant`-only.

This mirrors `openAiClientFromFieldConfig` / `activeAiProviderRuntimeConfig`
for the OpenAI/OpenRouter providers; the client it returns exposes the same
`client.messages()` surface the [`AnthropicBridge`](machine-learning.md#anthropicbridge-kt-anthropicbridge) drives.

## LlmBridge.kt { #llmbridge-kt }

Provider-neutral seam for the IDE agent loop.

Both the OpenAI/OpenRouter engine (`OpenAiIdeCodexBridge`, via [`OpenAiLlmBridge`](machine-learning.md#llmbridge-kt-openaillmbridge))
and the Anthropic engine ([`AnthropicBridge`](machine-learning.md#anthropicbridge-kt-anthropicbridge)) implement this, so `IdeChatHelpers`
and the installer can drive whichever provider is selected on /welcome without
caring which one is behind the interface.

The state/result types are the ones `OpenAiIdeCodexBridge` already defines — they
carry no OpenAI-SDK types in their signatures, so they double as the neutral
currency here. The typealiases below give them provider-neutral names without
moving the declarations (which 13 files reference).

### OpenAiLlmBridge { #llmbridge-kt-openaillmbridge }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">OpenAiLlmBridge</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">private</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="k">inner</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">OpenAiIdeCodexBridge</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">LlmBridge</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/models/LlmBridge/#L107)

Adapter that presents the existing (untouched) `OpenAiIdeCodexBridge` as an [`LlmBridge`](machine-learning.md#llmbridge-kt-llmbridge). Overrides carry no default values (Kotlin forbids that on an override); the defaults live on the interface and reach every call site typed as [`LlmBridge`](machine-learning.md#llmbridge-kt-llmbridge). A blank `startThread` instruction defers to the inner bridge's own default so existing behaviour is preserved exactly.

On house-machine-11 (2026-10-05) the forced final request also compacted the conversation (the next turn's input was 55k tokens, down from 100k); the next two turns, chained onto it, were offered every tool with tool_choice auto and answered "tool execution is still disabled here" without a call, though the first of them carried the reset note. 2026-10-04 had been the same, without the note. |

| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">branchState</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">name</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">save</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="p">(</span><span class="n">java</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">io</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">File</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="nc">Unit</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">restore</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="p">(</span><span class="n">java</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">io</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">File</span><span class="o">?</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="nc">Unit</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">onConflict</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">BranchConflict</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">BranchConflict</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">KEEP</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">resumeOnOpen</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">false</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/tools/AgentExtensions/#L109) | State of this box's that belongs to the conversation rather than the document — a canvas the agent paints on, a simulation it is steering. Field calls `save` (into a file it gives you) before and after every chat turn in this document, keeps each snapshot with that turn in the chat's session tree, and calls `restore` when the conversation moves: rewinding to a message restores the state from before that message, switching branch the state at that branch's end. `restore` gets `null` where the conversation has no snapshot (before the extension existed): start fresh, or keep what you have. The file is deleted when `restore` returns, so read it there. |

### DocumentToolRegistry { #boxaitools-kt-documenttoolregistry }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">object</span> <span class="nc">DocumentToolRegistry</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/tools/BoxAiTools/#L486)

Document-scoped registry of box-authored tools. A tool registered by any box in a document is visible to every agent anchored in that document — the in-app AI4 chat and external MCP users alike. Keyed by document path; tools remember their owning box id so `clearBox` can drop them on box disposal.

| --- | --- |
| [<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Box</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">stateTree</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">name</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">label</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">read</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="nc">StateTreeSnapshot</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">inspect</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="p">(</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">fork</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="p">(</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="o">?</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ai/tools/StateTreeBrowser/#L55) | Expose an existing history to AI4's States browser. Callbacks only read saved data; they must not restore state or run admission checks. `read` returns metadata; `inspect` reads one exact saved ID. Optional `fork` creates a named saved child and returns its ID without activation or restoration. Leave it null for histories that cannot safely retain branches. Re-running replaces this named provider and the run's lifecycle owns its registration. |

## neuralparticles.kt { #neuralparticles-kt }

Taking a small trained network to the GPU: [`MlpWeights`](machine-learning.md#neuralparticles-kt-mlpweights) is a flat, layer-major snapshot of a
multilayer perceptron's weights, and `MlpWeights.glsl` emits a GLSL function that evaluates the
same network out of a storage buffer.

What that buys is a particle whose update rule was *trained* rather than written. `flowMatch`
(see `flowmatching.kt`) already fits a velocity field `v(x, t)` in a couple of seconds of pure
Kotlin; a compute shader stepping a buffer of particles can evaluate that field per particle per
frame, provided the two sides agree about what the network *is*. This file is that agreement,
and `afield.examples.four.NeuralFieldParitySmoke` measures that it holds on real hardware.

Nothing here is particle-specific: a net that takes a position and returns a velocity, a net
that takes a neighbour offset and returns an interaction term, and a net that takes anything and
returns anything are all the same object. The particle system is what consumes it.

### Two comparisons, not one

There are two distinct errors between "the network Smile trained" and "the network the GPU
runs", they have very different sizes, and conflating them makes the unavoidable one look like
a bug.

- **Precision.** Smile evaluates in `Double`; a shader evaluates in `float`. Agreement is
  therefore limited to fp32 by construction — a few parts in a million, relative, and rather
  more for an output that is a cancelling sum. `MlpWeights.evaluate` is the fp32 reference *in
  Kotlin*, so this error can be measured on its own with no GPU present at all.
- **Transcription.** The order of the layers, the orientation of each weight matrix, the slope
  of the leaky ReLU, whether the output layer has an activation. Every one of these is either
  exactly right or grossly wrong, and a grossly wrong one still produces smooth, plausible,
  entirely fictional output.

So the GPU is compared against `MlpWeights.evaluate`, fp32 against fp32, where the only
remaining freedom is the order the hardware chooses to accumulate a dot product in; and
`evaluate` is compared against Smile separately. A single comparison against `Double` would
have to be loose enough to absorb the precision gap, which is a tolerance wide enough to hide a
transposed matrix in a small network.

### The weight layout

`MlpWeights.flat` runs layer by layer from the first hidden layer to the output layer. Each
layer contributes its weight matrix, row-major with one row per *output* neuron, then its bias
vector. So for a layer with `n` outputs over `p` inputs, the weight from input `i` to output `o`
is at `weightOffset(layer) + o * p + i`, and its bias is at `biasOffset(layer) + o`. The input
layer contributes nothing — it holds no weights.

This is the layout a shader wants to read, and it is also the layout Smile happens to store.
The two are not relied on to coincide: `VectorMLP.exportWeights` in `flowmatching.kt` reads
element by element through `DenseMatrix.get(row, column)` rather than copying memory, so a
change of storage order upstream cannot silently transpose the network.

## neuralparticles_system.kt { #neuralparticles-system-kt }

A particle system driven by a trained velocity field: [`ShaderNeuralParticles`](machine-learning.md#neuralparticles-system-kt-shaderneuralparticles) integrates a
buffer of particles along the field in a compute pass and draws the same allocation as points,
with no copy between the two.

`neuralparticles.kt` settles what a network *is* on both sides of the CPU/GPU line and emits
the GLSL that evaluates one; this file is what consumes that GLSL. The chain from a target
shape to a moving cloud is `flowMatch`, then `FlowMatchField.export()`, then
[`ShaderNeuralParticles`](machine-learning.md#neuralparticles-system-kt-shaderneuralparticles) and `installInto`. `afield.examples.four.NeuralParticlesSmoke` is the
GPU smoke over that whole path, and the `neural_particles` agent transcript is that chain as
three boxes.

Two of the design decisions reach the caller, so they are stated here rather than only on the
declarations that implement them:

- **Positions are stored in the training frame**, not in the coordinates the field was
  authored in, because integrating in input coordinates would convert into the frame and back
  out again on every step to reach the same answer. So [`NeuralParticleSettings`](machine-learning.md#neuralparticles-system-kt-neuralparticlesettings)'s `viewScale`
  and `viewCenter` are in normalised units, where a scale of about 2.6 frames a cloud of
  roughly unit variance.
- **A particle is travelling a journey, not wandering a force field.** A flow is a map: each
  particle goes from one specific source point to wherever the field takes it by `t = 1`, then
  starts again. That is why it carries a `start` and a `t`, and why `reset` has to seed from
  the field's own source cloud whenever the field has one.

Which settings are live follows from where each one is read. `particleCount` sizes the particle
buffer, the compute dispatch and the point mesh at construction, so it cannot be raised
afterwards, and `name` is written into the module and buffer names there. `phaseSpread`,
`sourceJitter` and `randomSeed` are read by `reset`, which fills the buffer, so changing one
takes a `reset` call. Everything else is read through a push-constant lambda every frame and
takes effect on the next one, including `stepsPerCycle` and `dwellCycles`.

The knobs [`ShaderNeuralParticles`](machine-learning.md#neuralparticles-system-kt-shaderneuralparticles) takes.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">name</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code> | Names the modules and buffers, so two systems in one renderer do not collide. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">particleCount</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | How many particles. A few hundred thousand is comfortable; see the class KDoc for cost. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">stepsPerCycle</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | Frames a particle takes to travel from `t = 0` to `t = 1`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">dwellCycles</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | How long a particle rests on the target once it arrives, as a multiple of the travel time. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">phaseSpread</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | How far apart in the cycle the particles start, as a fraction of a whole cycle. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">pointSize</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | Point size in pixels. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">sourceColor</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Vec4</span></code> | Colour a particle leaves the source with. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">targetColor</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Vec4</span></code> | Colour it arrives at the target with. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">intensity</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | Overall brightness. With additive blending this is the exposure control. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">arrivalBias</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | How strongly a particle's brightness is weighted toward the end of its journey, 0..1. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">viewScale</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | Half-height of the visible region, in the field's normalised units. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">viewCenter</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Vector2f</span></code> | Centre of the visible region, in the field's normalised units. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">flipY</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span></code> | Whether to negate `y` on the way to clip space. On by default. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">sourceJitter</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | Gaussian spread, in the field's normalised units, added to each particle's source point. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">randomSeed</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Long</span></code> | Seed for the source draw, so a scene reloads identically. |
